prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active forms, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B046 as a single prize part for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Round 1 showed that all six of us reach this position for stated scientific reasons and not by counting. The discovery is a complete chain from proglucagon processing and the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, through glucose-dependent insulin secretion, to central and gastric effects on appetite, and then to therapies with benefit shown in large independent trials for glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular outcomes and kidney disease. A discovery that visibly changed a field, was confirmed for decades and now underlies routine treatment meets the criteria as I understand them, and no maturity argument was raised against it in round 1. I also see a reason not to add a second part. A second part would force the physiology trio below three names or break the three-person cap. None of the proposed partners has an attribution that is clearly better than the GLP-1 one, and a single strong part reads more clearly than a diluted pair.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weakness, and round 1 did not remove it. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide relative to Habener's group is contested, and I cannot settle it from the supplied record. Habener and the early proglucagon sequencing groups are outside the credited names. Knudsen is excluded, so the prize can be read as honouring physiology while leaving out the step that produced the drugs patients receive. I accept both criticisms. I still think that crediting the principle and the identification of the active form is a more defensible reading of 'discovery' than crediting the later engineering of long-acting analogues. I would not claim the configuration is free of risk.

responses.point: Linnarsson says that my doubt about Mojsov also applies to B046, shares it, but would keep her because without the identification and synthesis of the active peptide the physiology and drug story lose their first link. He names Holst and Drucker alone as a thinner but defensible fallback. He also says my point about Eshhar is fair but does not sink B040.
responses.response: I accept the argument for Mojsov. The identity of the insulinotropic form is the step that makes the rest of the chain work, so removing her would weaken the discovery and not just tidy the attribution. I accept the Holst and Drucker pair as a fallback only if the record shows that her claim cannot be defended. I have seen nothing in the supplied material that shows this, and a contested priority is not the same as a refuted one. On B040 I stay where I was. I do not dismiss it, and I agree that a committee can credit the costimulated designs and their clinical proof without deciding who first built a chimeric receptor. Even so, the absence of Eshhar is a defect I would not set aside quietly, so B040 remains an alternative and not a second part.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius says that if the committee treats the industrial step as essential, the cleaner choice is to swap Mojsov for Knudsen. This would make the priority dispute disappear but would lose the peptide identification. She prefers to keep the discovery arc and describe the therapies in the citation. She also says the June and Sadelain pair resolves the three-name cap more cleanly than the six-name optogenetics list.
responses.response: I agree with the Mojsov-for-Knudsen analysis. That swap removes one dispute and creates a larger one, because it changes the prize from the discovery of the active hormone into a prize for drug design. I would not make the swap unless the committee decides as a matter of principle that the development step is the discovery. My citation therefore names the physiology of GLP-1 and its active forms and says the therapies were made possible by it. That acknowledges the clinical outcome without crediting the physiology laureates with the engineering. I also agree with her on allocation. A three-person cap fits the CAR-T pair better than it fits optogenetics, and I have therefore kept B040 ahead of B049 as the fallback.

responses.point: El-Manira keeps optogenetics as an alternative because the prize has honoured enabling methods with lasting effect. He now accepts that Hall with Sabatini is better than Hall with Schreiber for TOR, because TOR was found genetically and the mammalian mTOR and nutrient-sensing work is Sabatini's.
responses.response: On optogenetics, I accept that precedent for rewarding methods exists and that maturity is not the issue. The allocation is what stops me. He has said himself that his three-person cut cannot be defended as principled, and I agree. I would be uneasy ranking B049 as a second part while Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck have claims as strong as those of the three names he proposes. On TOR I have reconsidered. His argument that the physiological meaning of the pathway came from the mammalian work is persuasive, and Sandberg makes the same case. My round-1 preference for a lean Hall and Schreiber pair was a preference for a clean list, and it undervalued that work. If B015 returned I would now consider Hall with Sabatini, or all three. It stays outside my preferred configuration because I do not think it should displace GLP-1 this year.

responses.point: The chair (Svenningsson) would treat Habener as a limit of the supplied credit and not as a reason to hold back the prize, would word the citation around the physiology of GLP-1 and its active forms to avoid claiming sole priority for one group, and would support recording Habener's role in the committee's deliberations.
responses.response: I agree on all three points. We can only credit the names that we have evidence to support, and the citation should say what the three laureates discovered and not claim the whole field. I support recording Habener and the early proglucagon sequencing groups as limits of the supplied credit. That record is honest and does not change the configuration. I do not think it is a reason to delay, since the physiology is mature and the three named contributions are clearly part of the chain. I keep my doubt about B031 as a candidate for this year, not as a criticism of Walter and Mori. As I said in round 1, the two of us have worked together, so my judgment on B031 should be open to challenge. I would not object to it in a later year once ISRIB or IRE1-directed therapies show benefit.

responses.point: Sandberg disagrees with my Hall and Schreiber allocation for TOR and argues that the mammalian mTORC1 and mTORC2 architecture and nutrient sensing came mainly from Sabatini. He supports B040 as June and Sadelain only, and would accept a third name only if the citation said adoptive cell therapy and engineered T cells.
responses.response: His TOR point is correct and I have conceded it above. I should have credited the mammalian work, which is what connects TOR to human physiology. On B040 I accept the June and Sadelain pair as the better attribution and I would not add Rosenberg unless the committee reframed the achievement as engineered T-cell therapy in general. That is a different discovery from CAR design, and the citation would have to say so. I remain concerned about Eshhar. If the committee ever moves from B046 to B040, I would want that omission recorded openly.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide, relative to Habener's group, can be defended well enough to keep her in the trio. I cannot settle this from the supplied record.
Whether the committee will accept a prize that credits the physiology and leaves out Knudsen, or will think the citation underweights the drug development that reached patients.
Whether the absence of Eshhar from B040 is a flaw that should rule it out as an alternative, as opposed to one that should only be recorded.
Whether the TOR allocation should be Hall with Sabatini, Hall with Schreiber, or all three, if B015 returns in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: My profile records about twenty co-authored works with Per Svenningsson, who chairs the committee, and one with Abdel El Manira (2009). I regard these as collaborations that do not require recusal, and I disclose them again. I mention my earlier co-authorship with Ronald Evans for completeness. Neither is related to any shortlisted candidate. I have changed my mind on one point, the TOR allocation, because of the arguments of El-Manira and Sandberg, and I have not changed my preferred configuration. My research field of nuclear receptors and dopamine neuron development is not covered by any shortlisted candidate. I have no documented link to any person credited on the shortlist, so my disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
